titre: The “Council of Jamnia”: A Synod That Did Not Close the Canon
accroche: A council of rabbis is said to have fixed the Hebrew Bible around the year 90: the idea dates from 1871 and its sources do not support it.
contenu_vulgarise:
“Around the year 90, a council of rabbis gathered at Jamnia closed the canon of the Hebrew Bible.” This sentence long appeared in introductions to the Old Testament. It describes an assembly that no ancient text speaks of as a council.

## An Idea Born in the 19th Century

Jamnia, or Yavneh, is a locality in Palestine where Jewish masters gathered after the destruction of Jerusalem in 70. The idea of a council that would have ruled on the sacred books was formulated in 1871 by the Jewish historian Heinrich Graetz. For him, it was the last of the three stages in the canonization of the Jewish Scriptures. He imagined seventy-two masters examining the texts and questioning witnesses, then deciding by majority in favor of the Song of Songs and Ecclesiastes.

The hypothesis flourished, to the point of becoming the dominant opinion for much of the 20th century.

## What the Texts Say

In 1964, Jack P. Lewis published in the *Journal of Bible and Religion* an article titled “What Do We Mean By Jabneh?” His finding, as Albert Sundberg summarizes it: Jewish sources preserve an echo of debates about certain books, but canonicity was not at stake, and these debates are not tied to Yavneh. No ancient text describes a session, a vote, a fixed list.

The thesis has since been largely abandoned. F. F. Bruce considers it “probably unwise” to speak of a council or synod of Jamnia fixing the canon. The date at which the Hebrew Bible was definitively fixed is still debated.

## What This Shifts

One moment was imagined: a room, a vote, a closing. The evidence suggests another process, slower and without a conductor, in which texts are recognized first through use. The “council” is a model borrowed from the history of Christianity and projected onto 1st-century Judaism.

This textbook story illustrates a common failing: when the sources give neither a session, nor a list, nor a vote, one is supposed, because a dated event is easier to remember than a diffuse process. Nothing rules out that masters discussed books at Yavneh; what the texts do not allow is to make those discussions the official closing of a canon.

A precise date is reassuring; here it took the place of the question.

carte.punch: The council that supposedly closed the Hebrew Bible around the year 90 was imagined in 1871.
carte.idee: The historian Heinrich Graetz proposed in 1871 a council of Jamnia that would have fixed the Jewish canon. In 1964, Jack P. Lewis showed that the sources do not support it: debates about certain books exist, but they are not tied to Yavneh, and canonicity was not at stake in them.
carte.source_courte: J. P. Lewis, Journal of Bible and Religion, 1964

quiz.question: What does Jack P. Lewis's 1964 article on Jamnia show?
choix: That the council really took place around the year 90 under the leadership of a patriarch
That canonicity was not at stake in the attested debates, and that they are not tied to Yavneh
That the Hebrew canon was fixed much earlier, in the time of Ezra
That the council of Jamnia was convened against the Christians
quiz.explication: Lewis concludes that the debates about certain books were not about canonicity and are not tied to Yavneh. He does not date the canon, and the thesis of a council does not come from the sources.

quiz_supplementaire.question: Who formulated the hypothesis of a council of Jamnia, and when?
choix: Jerome of Stridon, in the 4th century
quiz_supplementaire.explication: Graetz proposed it in 1871. Bruce is a later critic of the thesis; neither Jerome nor Josephus describes such a council.

quiz_supplementaire.question: Which books did Graetz imagine being decided by majority at Jamnia?
choix: The Song of Songs and Ecclesiastes
quiz_supplementaire.explication: In Graetz's reconstruction, the debate concerned the Song of Songs and Ecclesiastes, two disputed books. The other pairs are not part of it.
